claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9111 §1: 'An HTTP cache is a local store of response messages and the subsystem that controls storage, retrieval, and deletion of messages in it. A cache stores cacheable responses to reduce the response time and network bandwidth consumption on future equivalent requests.' §4.2: 'When a response is fresh, it can be used to satisfy subsequent requests without contacting the origin server, thereby improving efficiency.'

RFC 9111 §1: 'A shared cache is a cache that stores responses for reuse by more than one user; shared caches are usually (but not always) deployed as a part of an intermediary. A private cache, in contrast, is dedicated to a single user; often, they are deployed as a component of a user agent.' Same section: 'A fresh response can therefore reduce both latency and network overhead each time the cache reuses it.' The network-trip half follows from the placement: a store inside the user agent is reached without leaving the machine.

RFC 9111 §2: 'Most commonly, caches store the successful result of a retrieval request: i.e., a 200 (OK) response to a GET request ... However, it is also possible to store redirects, negative results ..., incomplete results ..., and responses to methods other than GET if the method's definition allows such caching'. RFC 9110 §9.3.3: 'Responses to POST requests are only cacheable when they include explicit freshness information ... In contrast, a POST request cannot be satisfied by a cached POST response because POST is potentially unsafe'. The hedge 'normally' is exactly right.

RFC 9111 §5.2.2.1: 'The max-age response directive indicates that the response is to be considered stale after its age is greater than the specified number of seconds.' Argument syntax: delta-seconds. §4.2.1 calculating freshness_lifetime: 'If the max-age response directive (Section 5.2.2.1) is present, use its value'. §4.2: 'A fresh response is one whose age has not yet exceeded its freshness lifetime' and 'When a response is fresh, it can be used to satisfy subsequent requests without contacting the origin server.'

RFC 9111 §4.2.4: 'A stale response is one that either has explicit expiry information or is allowed to have heuristic expiry calculated, but is not fresh' and 'A cache MUST NOT generate a stale response unless it is disconnected or doing so is explicitly permitted by the client or origin server (e.g., by the max-stale request directive ...)'. §4.2: 'Compliant caches will normally validate a stale cached response before reusing it for subsequent requests'. Nothing in §3 or §4 requires a stale entry to be deleted.

RFC 9110 §8.8.3: 'The ETag field in a response provides the current entity tag for the selected representation, as determined at the conclusion of handling the request. An entity tag is an opaque validator for differentiating between multiple representations of the same resource, regardless of whether those multiple representations are due to resource state changes over time, content negotiation ..., or both.'

RFC 9110 §13.1.2: 'the client SHOULD generate an If-None-Match header field containing a list of those entity tags when making a GET request; this allows recipient servers to send a 304 (Not Modified) response'. Evaluation rule 2: 'the condition is false if one of the listed tags matches the entity tag of the selected representation.' RFC 9111 §4.3.1: a cache 'MUST send the relevant entity tags (using If-Match, If-None-Match, or If-Range) if the entity tags were provided in the stored response(s) being validated.'

RFC 9110 §13.1.2: if the condition evaluates to false 'the origin server MUST respond with either a) the 304 (Not Modified) status code if the request method is GET or HEAD'; otherwise the method runs normally. §15.4.5: 'A 304 response is terminated by the end of the header section; it cannot contain content or trailers.' RFC 9111 §4.3.3: 'A 304 (Not Modified) response status code indicates that the stored response can be updated and reused'; and for a full response, 'the cache MUST use the full response to satisfy the request.'

RFC 9110 places 304 in §15.4 Redirection 3xx, not in §15.3 Successful 2xx. §15.4.5: 'there is no need for the server to transfer a representation of the target resource because the request indicates that the client, which made the request conditional, already has a valid representation; the server is therefore redirecting the client to make use of that stored representation as if it were the content of a 200 (OK) response'; and 'it cannot contain content or trailers.'

RFC 9111 §4.2.2: a cache 'MAY assign a heuristic expiration time when an explicit time is not specified, employing algorithms that use other field values (such as the Last-Modified time) ... This specification does not provide specific algorithms'. The claim drops a condition stated in the same section: 'heuristics can only be used on responses without explicit freshness whose status codes are defined as heuristically cacheable ... and on responses without explicit freshness that have been marked as explicitly cacheable'. For /index.html the code is 200, so the lesson's own case holds.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: A response with no Cache-Control field is not thereby uncacheable: when its status code is one defined as heuristically cacheable (200 is), a cache MAY assign a heuristic expiration time from other fields such as Last-Modified. RFC 9111 prescribes no algorithm, so two caches may keep the same page fresh for different lengths of time.

claim_verdicts.evidence: Caddy docs, directives/handle: 'Evaluates a group of directives mutually exclusively from other handle blocks at the same level of nesting'; 'only the first matching handle block will be evaluated'. directives/header: 'Manipulates HTTP response header fields. It can set, add, and delete header values'; bare 'header <field> <value>' overwrites. Caddyfile@stage-0 lines 70-74 hold the file's only Cache-Control; header appears elsewhere only for Content-Type, Location and Set-Cookie (lines 37-38, 42, 46, 53, 59).

Execution evidence: outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/cache-headers.txt@stage-0 shows 'Etag: ...' for /cached.html although lines 70-74 of the Caddyfile set only Cache-Control there, so file_server is what supplies it; outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/raw-request.txt shows Etag and Last-Modified on /index.html, also file_server. WebFetch of caddyserver.com/docs/caddyfile/directives/file_server returns no occurrence of ETag/Etag at all, so the ledger's 'documentation does not state how the value is computed' is if anything understated.

outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/cache-headers.txt@stage-0 is exactly 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK / Cache-Control: max-age=60 / Etag: ...', then '   304', then '   no Cache-Control header, so every cache decides for itself'. .github/workflows/ci.yml runs ./scripts/capture-output.sh --all and then 'git diff --exit-code -- outputs/', against caddy:2.10.0 (docker-compose.yml), the version pinned in versions.yaml. I could not re-run it here: the Docker daemon was unreachable (open //./pipe/dockerDesktopLinuxEngine failed).

outputs/unstable.regex@stage-0 header: 'One Perl regular expression per line. Whatever a line matches is replaced by "..." in every captured output, so that a re-run of the same script produces the same file'; it contains the line '^Etag: \K.*$'. scripts/capture-output.sh runs the script, then a Perl block that applies every pattern to the captured file before it is written. ci.yml then runs 'git diff --exit-code -- outputs/'.

scripts/http/cache-headers.sh@stage-0 lines 13-16: etag=$(curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null http://localhost:8080/cached.html | grep -i '^etag:' | tr -d '\r' | cut -d' ' -f2) followed immediately by curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '   %{http_code}\n' -H "If-None-Match: $etag" http://localhost:8080/cached.html. The validator is read from a fresh response in the same sequence, so it cannot be an older one; a client that stored a response earlier can be.

RFC 9111 §1: 'The goal of HTTP caching is significantly improving performance by reusing a prior response message to satisfy a current request ... A fresh response can therefore reduce both latency and network overhead each time the cache reuses it.' §4.2: 'Generally, origin servers will assign future explicit expiration times to responses in the belief that the representation is not likely to change in a semantically significant way before the expiration time is reached' — a belief, which is the staleness risk the claim names.

RFC 9111 §4.2: 'When a response is fresh, it can be used to satisfy subsequent requests without contacting the origin server'. §4 lists what a cache checks before reuse (URI, method, nominated fields, no-cache, freshness); none of it concerns whether the visitor has been there before. §1 covers the copies the reader does not control: 'A shared cache is a cache that stores responses for reuse by more than one user; shared caches are usually (but not always) deployed as a part of an intermediary.'

scripts/http/cache-headers.sh@stage-0: every step is its own curl with -o /dev/null, nothing is written to disk, and only the shell variable $etag crosses a command, so no response is stored for max-age=60 to govern. The three steps run consecutively with no sleep, and outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/cache-headers.txt records '   304' under step 2, so that request left and was answered well inside the 60 s window. Re-execution was not possible here (Docker daemon unreachable).

RFC 9111 §5.2.1.4: 'The no-cache request directive indicates that the client prefers a stored response not be used to satisfy the request without successful validation on the origin server.' That is a stated preference, not the prohibition 'tells caches not to' implies; §4's reuse conditions name the no-cache response directive (§5.2.2.4), not the request one. The second half is exact — §4.2: 'Note that freshness applies only to cache operation; it cannot be used to force a user agent to refresh its display or reload a resource.'
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: A request may itself ask that a stored response not be reused: the no-cache request directive indicates that the client prefers a stored response not be used to satisfy the request without successful validation on the origin server, which is what a deliberate refresh can send; freshness applies only to cache operation and cannot force a user agent to reload a resource.

claim_verdicts.evidence: scripts/up.sh@stage-0: 'Start the Đơn Hàng lab: the static site, the database and the lab box', then docker compose up -d --build --wait over services lab, web (caddy:2.10.0) and db (postgres:17.6-alpine) — the first half is exact. The second half is off by position: the re-execution is line 5, '[ -f /.dockerenv ] || exec "$(dirname "$0")/../lab-run.sh" "$0" "$@"', not the script's first line (line 1 is the shebang; line 4, the excerpt's first line, is a comment), and it fires only when the script is not already inside the box.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: scripts/up.sh starts the lab with docker compose (services lab, web, db: the static site, the database and the lab box). Line 5 of cache-headers.sh — the second line of the excerpt shown — re-executes the script inside the lab box via scripts/lab-run.sh unless it is already running there, so with Docker installed and the lab up the reader starts nothing else by hand.

claim_verdicts.evidence: Step 1: curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null ... | grep -Ei '^(HTTP/|Cache-Control:|Etag:)'. Step 2: curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '   %{http_code}\n' -H "If-None-Match: $etag" .... The options do differ (-D - dumps the header section, -w prints only the code, -o /dev/null discards the body in both), and outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/cache-headers.txt prints three header lines under step 1 and '   304' under step 2. Caveat: which three header lines appear is the doing of the grep filter, not of curl's options alone.

issues.text: The stated cause is not the operative one, and the same paragraph contradicts it two sentences later: "it reads the current `Etag` immediately before quoting it back, so it can never hold an old one". Step 2 re-reads the Etag inside each run, so run 2 prints `304` whether or not anything touched the file between the runs. As written, the reader is taught that an untouched file is what produces the `304` — the exact inference the paragraph then tries to block.
issues.quote: Expected result: the same `304` both times, because nothing between the two runs touched the file.
issues.fix: Remove the false cause: "Expected result: the same `304` both times — step 2 reads the current `Etag` and quotes it straight back, so the origin always finds a match." Keep the following "Note what the script does *not* prove" sentence, which then follows from it instead of contradicting it.

issues.text: Unlisted claim: two specific assertions about the example repository at tag stage-0 — that no application sits behind the site, and that Caddy answers a fixed set of paths — appear in no entry of `.meta.json`, although claims 11-15 and 18-21 record repository facts of exactly this kind. Both are true (Caddyfile@stage-0 header: "There is no application behind these answers yet; that arrives at stage-1"; the routes are a closed list), but the ledger does not show they were checked.
issues.quote: The lab site has no application behind it at this tag; Caddy, the lab's web server, answers a fixed set of paths, one written for this lesson.
issues.fix: Add a claim to `.meta.json` (kind `behavior`, version_key `caddy`, section 5): "At tag stage-0 the lab site is served by Caddy alone with no application behind it; the Caddyfile answers a closed set of paths, one of which (/cached.html) exists for this lesson." source_hint: examples/don-hang Caddyfile@stage-0, header comment and route list.

issues.text: The `/index.html` response does carry reuse machinery: outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/raw-request.txt@stage-0 shows `Etag: ...` and `Last-Modified: ...` on it, and RFC 9111 §4.2.2 names Last-Modified as the field heuristics use. What the response omits is `Cache-Control`, which is exactly what step 3 of the script tests (`grep -qi '^cache-control:'`). "Says nothing about reuse" overstates the omission and does not match §5, which says only that the page has no `Cache-Control` line.
issues.quote: Then you ask for `/index.html`, which answers `200` and says nothing about reuse.
issues.fix: Narrow the clause to what the script tests: "which answers `200` and says nothing about how long it may be reused".

issues.text: "Forbidding" is stronger than the specification. RFC 9111 §5.2.1.4: "The no-cache request directive indicates that the client prefers a stored response not be used to satisfy the request without successful validation on the origin server." A preference, not a prohibition: §4's conditions on reuse name the no-cache response directive (§5.2.2.4), not the request one. Claim 19 in `.meta.json` carries the same overstatement ("tells caches not to").
issues.quote: that request can carry a directive forbidding reuse without checking with the origin
issues.fix: Write "that request can carry a directive asking caches not to reuse a stored copy without checking with the origin first", and take claim 19's suggested_text into `.meta.json`.

issues.text: Off-by-one against the source. The script's first line is `#!/usr/bin/env bash` (line 1) and the first line of the excerpt is the comment on line 4; the line that re-executes the script inside the lab box is line 5, `[ -f /.dockerenv ] || exec "$(dirname "$0")/../lab-run.sh" "$0" "$@"`. Claim 20 in `.meta.json` repeats the same "the first line".
issues.quote: the script's first line moves itself into that box
issues.fix: Say "the second line of the block above moves the script into that box" (or "the `exec` line moves it there"), and correct claim 20 in `.meta.json` the same way — see its suggested_text.

issues.text: Section 5 told me plainly that each step is its own command that keeps nothing from the one before, so there is no stored copy anywhere in this run. Then the Expected result tells me that what I display has to come from the copy I was already holding — but I am holding nothing. I stopped and re-read both sections trying to decide whether I had misunderstood section 5 or whether this sentence is about a browser and not about my run. It is the sentence that tells me what my result means, so I could not leave it unresolved.
issues.quote: it sent no page, so anything you display has to come from the copy you were already holding
issues.fix: Move the sentence off the reader's own run: "it sent no page, so a browser in this position could only show the copy it was already holding — here, with nothing stored, you see only the code."

issues.text: The first sentence hands me two words about the example repository — "tag stage-0" and "a fresh clone" — and neither is ever explained. I guessed that a tag names a version of the repository and a clone is my own copy of it, and the guess carried me through, but I was guessing on line one, and Try it assumes I am at that state.
issues.quote: (tag `stage-0`, the state a fresh clone is already in)
issues.fix: Say it in that same parenthesis without new words: "(at `stage-0`, the point in the example repository this lesson uses — a newly downloaded copy is already there)".

issues.text: "A box to run commands in" and "that box" are the only names for the thing my commands run in, and I do not know what a box is: another machine, another program, a folder? The prose does say what the line is for, so I was not stuck, but I could not tell what I would need on my own machine before the script works.
issues.quote: `scripts/up.sh` starts the site and a box to run commands in
issues.fix: Gloss it once where it first appears: "`scripts/up.sh` starts the site and, beside it, a small separate environment that already has the commands these scripts use".

issues.text: Step 1 tells me to note the `Etag` value and step 2 tells me to compare the two runs, but Expected result only speaks about the `304`. I wrote a value down and was never told what it should look like the second time, so if my two `Etag` values differed I would not know whether I had broken something or seen the point of the exercise.

issues.text: "Directive" is a new word for what section 4 called an instruction, and "forbidding reuse without checking with the origin" reads two ways: forbidding all reuse, or forbidding only reuse that skips the check. I read the sentence twice and settled on the second reading from the `304` story earlier, not from the sentence itself.
issues.quote: that request can carry a directive forbidding reuse without checking with the origin
issues.fix: Use the lesson's own word and one order of clauses: "that request can carry an instruction telling every store on the way to check with the origin before reusing anything".

issues.text: The prose narrates every arrow except `K-->>C: 200 and the page, copy kept`: the paragraph ends with the cache keeping the copy and never says the client got the page on that first exchange.
